text: You sold a $4 hot dog.
The customer handed you a 5 and told you to keep the change.
You put the bill in the cash box and checked your phone.
Your daughter had gotten her first hit in the first game of the season.
Emily had sent you a video.
You replayed it twice just to see where the ball went.
On the third replay, you noticed the spot they'd saved for you on the bleachers.
When you bought the hot dog cart, working Saturdays had sounded like a pretty good idea.
You're 34.
You live outside Columbus, Ohio, in a house with a two-car garage that fits exactly
one car.
The other side is full of bikes, Christmas lights, and a shelf you've been meaning to put up for
six years.
You work weekdays at a distribution center.
Your wife, Emily, schedules appointments at a dental office.
Your daughter, Ellie, is 9.
Your son, Ben, is 6.
As far as Ben is concerned, putting anything besides ketchup on a hot dog is just a slower
way of throwing it away.
It started on a Sunday evening.
You were grilling hot dogs for the neighbors in front of the garage.
Mike from across the street reached for his third and said,
You ought to sell these.
You went inside and told Emily.
She shut the dishwasher.
Is Mike going to pay for them?
The next night, you sat down at the kitchen table and ran the numbers.
You pulled up a listing for a used cart.
Emily pulled up the household budget.
You had $18,000 in savings.
You agreed to leave half of it alone.
The air conditioner was 18 years old.
At the last service call, the technician had written a date on the unit.
Neither of you had asked what the date meant.
You found a cart near Dayton for $5,400.
The seller pulled the lid for the relish bin out of his trunk and handed it to you.
Don't leave this open when it's windy.
That's my second one.
A propane tank, a cooler, thermometers, and the parts you needed for the hand washing
station ran you $780.
Insurance, permits, and the first payments on a shared prep kitchen came to $1,140.
The sign, the card reader, and your first round of supplies and packaging cost $680.
$8,000 total.
You hadn't sold a single hot dog, and you already knew how many $4 bills it would take
to get your money back.
$2,000, if $4 bills existed.
You put Ellie in charge of the name.
She came back with three options.
The first was dad dogs.
The second was dad dogs too.
The third was dad dogs again, this time with a picture of a dog.
You went with the third one.
Emily sent the drawing to the sign shop.
When you mounted the sign, one of the screws went right through the dog's tail.
The first time Ellie saw it, she colored the screw black.
The dog had its tail back.
You kept the menu short.
A classic was $4.
Mustard, onions, and relish.
A chili cheese dog was $6.
A classic with chips and a canned drink was $7.
At the bottom of the board, you added Ben's plane.
When Ben saw his name up there, he spent a week arguing that family should eat for free.
Eventually, he settled for himself.
Your first Saturday, you got a spot at the neighborhood farmer's market.
You were up at 5.30.
You picked up your supplies from the shared kitchen, pulled into your spot,
and lined up your mustard bottles at 9.
At 9.45, you still hadn't sold a thing.
The coffee cart by the entrance had 14 people in line.
A guy stopped in front of you, looked at the menu,
and asked the vendor next door how much the tomatoes were.
Your first customer showed up at 11.03.
He wanted two classics.
Hold the onions on the second one.
You put onions on both.
You made the second one over.
You ate the one with onions for lunch.
You took in $312 that day.
After food, the spot fee, card fees, and gas, you had $121 left.
You'd been gone 9 hours.
Emily asked how you did while you were standing in the kitchen.
She said, that's good.
Then she pulled Ellie's jersey out of the washing machine.
Do you know what time first pitches next Saturday?
You didn't.
You checked.
The best hour at the farmer's market was 11 too.
All through May, you worked the farmer's market on Saturdays
and a home improvement store parking lot on Sundays.
The store manager gave you a spot by the entrance.
People came in for paint and left with hot dogs.
One guy came two Sundays in a row.
Both times he said the same thing.
My wife made lunch.
Don't let her see this.
The second week, his wife showed up too.
She ordered a chili cheese dog.
You did $3840 in sales in May.
After operating expenses, you had $1210 left before taxes.
Pretty good for a first month.
Most Sunday nights though, Emily was setting four plates on the table
while you were still washing out the bins on the cart.
One night, Ben turned a bowl upside down over your plate.
Emily asked him what he was doing, keeping it warm for dad.
In June, you booked your first big event, a neighborhood summer festival.
The organizer said 700 people had come the year before.
You bought 240 hot dogs.
Emily asked, how many of those 700 people bought food?
You texted the organizer again.
He didn't know.
They'd counted the wristbands they handed out at the gate.
It started raining at two.
It let up at four.
The band that was supposed to go on at five canceled.
By the time you got home, you'd sold 68 hot dogs.
The spot alone had cost you $250.
You lost $190 that day.
On the way home, you stopped at a gas station and bought two coffees.
One for Emily.
She was already asleep when you got in.
In the morning, there was a note next to the cup.
Next time, let's know how many were getting paid for before we go.
The next job came from Mike.
The auto shop where he worked was throwing a summer lunch for its employees.
The manager wanted meals for 80 people at nine bucks a head.
A hot dog, chips, a drink, and two hours of service.
You put all 80 meals in the agreement.
67 people showed up.
The manager set the rest aside for the evening shift.
For the first time, you knew how much you'd bring in before you went shopping.
You kept $390 after expenses.
And you were home by three.
Ellie was hitting softballs in the driveway.
You grabbed your glove and took a few steps back.
You missed the first one.
Missed the second one too.
They don't come at you that fast in a game, you said.
Yeah, they do, Ellie said.
You weren't there.
On the 4th of July, you booked a spot at the town fireworks show.
This time, you asked the organizer three questions.
How many meals sold last year?
How many food vendors are coming?
Where are you putting the carts?
The spot cost $350.
While Emily was paying, she zoomed in on the map.
You were right between the parking lot and the lawn.
Everybody carrying a folding chair out of their trunk would walk right past you.
By seven, you had 20 people in line.
You could keep up with the orders.
Your card reader couldn't.
Everyone pulled out their phones at once and the connection dropped.
The first two customers found cash in their wallets.
The third dumped a pocket full of change on the counter.
The fourth got out of line.
Emily grabbed a sheet of paper, wrote down the prices, and waved the cash customers over.
She took orders until the reader came back online.
You kept opening buns.
You sold 286 hot dogs that night.
You took in $1,790.
After the event fee, supplies, card fees, and gas, you kept $805.
It was your best day in six months.
On the drive home, Ben was asleep in the back seat.
Ellie had watched the fireworks with her grandma.
Dad, did you see the finale?
You said you did.
She tried to describe it anyway.
The red ones had these white ones that burst out of the middle.
You'd seen two flashes reflected in the metal lid of the cart.
One hot afternoon in August, you sold four hot dogs in an hour outside the home improvement store.
On the first Friday night in September,
you sold 93 in 40 minutes outside a high school football game.
The following week, you went back with twice as many buns.
The home team was playing away.
That was the night you learned to check the schedule.
The next morning, you made Ben toast with some of the leftover buns.
That's my hot dog bun, he said.
Yep, he finished it.
Can you put a hot dog in the next one?
At the end of September, Emily set a sheet of paper on the kitchen table.
The hot dog, bun, toppings, and wrapper for a $4 classic cost you $1.32.
Once the card fee came out, you had about $2.50 left.
You still had to pay for the spot, fill the propane tank, and tow the cart there.
If the market charged $85 for a spot, you had to sell 34 classics just to cover that fee.
On a rainy day, it could take you all day to sell 34.
At a company lunch, the manager paid for 80 people whether 80 people showed up or not.
At the end of October, you added up 6 months of sales.
After food, event fees, card fees, the shared kitchen,
fuel, and the rest of your operating costs, you had $9,420 before taxes.
Take out the $8,000 you put in up front, and you were ahead by $1,420.
You still had to set money aside for taxes.
Emily turned the laptop toward you.
You looked at the sales total.
Then you pulled up the calendar.
You'd opened the cart 19 Saturdays since May.
You'd watched four of Ellie's games from start to finish.
You booked two company lunches for November.
Both on weekdays.
Then you opened a message from the farmer's market.
Last, outdoor market of the year.
They'd saved your usual spot.
Ellie's last game of the season was that same morning.
This time you knew when first pitch was.
At 5 to 11 on Saturday, the hot dog cart is in the garage.
You're in the bleachers.
Emily walks up with two coffees.
Ben's sitting next to you, unwrapping something in foil.
You made it for him before you left the house.
Ketchup, a $4 Ben's plane.
Ellie swings and misses at the first pitch.
On the second, she sends the ball past third base.
She touches first and turns toward the bleachers.
You raise your hand.
This time, you can hear yourself cheering in the video.
So where would you set up your hot dog cart?
At the same farmer's market every Saturday?
Or at events where you know how many meals you're getting paid for?
And while we're here, is Ben right about ketchup?
Let me know in the comments.

If I pick your idea, I'll give you a shout out in the video.
